Nora had borrowed in twenty twenty-three, at seven point six two percent. At the February rate, a new loan would have cut her payment by four hundred fifty-nine dollars a month.

[softly] She didn't take it.

By late September, the rate was back above seven percent, for the first time since January twenty twenty-five.

S05.text_sent:
You may have heard that a refinance only pays off once rates fall a full percentage point below yours. We use that one-point line as a test. And for Nora, rates did cross that line. In twenty twenty-six, the average spent twenty-nine weeks at least a full point below her rate. At the February low, the gap was one point six four points. After the week ending July twenty-third, twenty twenty-six, the gap never again reached a full point, and the window closed.

Whether it opens again, we can't tell you: everything in this story is history, not a forecast, and it covers the U.S. only.

The one-point line says no. Her cut falls short. Simple division says yes: five thousand one hundred twenty-four dollars divided by two hundred twenty-one dollars is about twenty-four months.

Neither is quite right. The one-point line never looks at the bill. And the division leaves something out.

S10.text_sent:
Nora has made thirty-five payments on her old loan, one a month since she moved in. With each one, a little more goes to paying down what she owes. A refinance starts a fresh thirty-year clock, and in the early years of any mortgage, most of each payment goes to interest. So the new loan pays down her balance more slowly than the old one would have. By month twenty-four, she owes one thousand one hundred thirty-three dollars more than if she had kept the old loan.

[thoughtful] If she sold the house then, that one thousand one hundred thirty-three dollars would come out of her sale money, so it cancels part of what she has saved. Her savings need a few more months to cover it, and the gap keeps growing a little while they do. [serious] Count it, and break-even moves from month twenty-four to month thirty.
